rv.q: This Oklahoma! is no stuffy academic revisionist exercise — it’s a theatrical blow-out.
Purists will sniff anyway, but for audiences open to experiencing Rodgers & Hammerstein’s Oklahoma! from a fresh perspective, director Daniel Fish’s probing revamp will be a revelation.
But this production impressively harvests all that Oklahoma! has to offer.
The wonder of this production is that so much of the joy and optimism of the original work still shines bright through the darkness.
This is a production that takes the familiar and makes it feel dangerous again
Daniel Fish's radical reimagining of the Rodgers and Hammerstein classic is both faithful to the original and completely its own thing.
Oklahoma! it remains, but there's nothing corny about it.
What’s best in this “Oklahoma!” is the morally ambiguous cue Fish develops so smartly from Rodgers and Hammerstein’s own narrative impulses.

Where intentional or not, Fish and his unforgiving team of designers have forged an "Oklahoma" for a digital America where everyone has their confirmatory feeds and dealing with another human can mean starring down the barrel of a gun.
Too often I found myself weighing the moments of inspiration against the moments of bewildering distraction.
Everything you cherish about this classic has been taken out behind the barn and shot, replaced by an auteur’s bag of tricks and a thesis on gun control and westward expansion.

That darkness is not just confined to one scene but is spiritually draped over Daniel Fish’s daring, brilliant, utterly absorbing re-interpretation of Rodgers and Hammerstein’s 1943 musical play; a first in itself.

This Oklahoma! is unquestionably a triumph, one that honors Rodgers and Hammerstein's original while making it feel urgent and necessary for today.
This makes it the most engrossing musical currently on Broadway and a must-see.

And if you listen real hard, you’ll find that in this “Oklahoma!” like the rest of the modern world, no one really gets to ride off into the sunset.
So even if you'd rather see Oklahoma! back on Broadway in its cornier but sunnier and more traditional format, don't miss this new-fangled version.
I could enjoy this 'Oklahoma' without much reservation.
Even the title song, usually imbued with the sunny, can-do optimism of the war era, becomes in this revelatory production less an anthem of pride than of stubborn defiance.
This Oklahoma! doesn't just deconstruct Rodgers and Hammerstein's 1943 musical — it excavates it, examining what lies beneath all that cornpone Americana.
This is not a piece of theater that allows you to sit back and be entertained.

Fun is not joy, though, and too often in this Oklahoma! I found myself missing the sense of magic and transcendence that comes from seeing life, with all its pleasure and pain, elevated by this particular art form.

Sexually charged and presented with a striking naturalism, this bold new production is a revelation and a must-see.

Oklahoma!'s eery timeliness is proof of the universality of the show.

This reimagining of “Oklahoma!” adds very little – if anything at all – to the original musical or any of its previous revivals.
Mr. Fish has stripped Oklahoma! of any breath, color, insight, delicacy, intimacy, choreography, costumes, subtle acting, and beautiful singing.
